description: The Galagans (Málaga + a nod to the classic arcade shooter) are building AI-powered health monitoring for astronauts: real-time vitals, early anomaly detection, and clear dashboards that work in deep space. We're looking for coders, data nerds, hardware tinkerers, and designers to join the mission.
summary:
Bound for Mars, the crew is its own first doctor. A message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, sometimes the link drops entirely, and bone loss, blood clots or reactivated viruses give no early warning. NASA-STD-3001 already requires crews to assess, monitor and trend their health on board [V1 3004], yet the only crew health app flying today, CNES EveryWear, records data without interpreting it.

Six Dots Companion turns that data into clear next steps. A two-minute daily check-in on an offline tablet, plus readings from flight-class devices, is compared with the astronaut’s own pre-flight normal or a sourced NASA or clinical limit. Every alert explains itself: what changed, why it matters, which of 23 cited rules decided it, and what to do now, following NASA’s escalation ladder from self-care to the Crew Medical Officer, a private medical conference or the ground.

The rules decide; AI never diagnoses. An on-board voice model only turns speech into commands, with no internet. A small six-dot display shows status at a glance, and streaks reward reporting symptoms, never good numbers.

Everything above runs today. Trigger a cabin air fault in the simulator and watch CO₂ climb, then SpO₂ fall and heart rate rise, as the tablet raises and explains each alert in real time.
details:
On long missions, health trouble starts small: a headache nobody mentions, a reading that slowly drifts. Astronauts under-report symptoms for fear of losing flights, and Earth limits misfire in space. Six Dots Companion makes reporting worth it and every alert worth reading.

Six simulated flight-class devices stream readings to an offline iPad app that runs a sourced rule table on board. Each body system gets a level against the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline, and a packet for the flight surgeon waits until the link to Earth is up.

Six alert levels follow the caution and warning classes astronauts already train on: Nominal, To do, Watch, Check, Treat and Emergency. Each has an icon and a word, never colour alone. Colour appears nowhere else in the app, so any colour on screen means act.

Our reward system makes telling the truth the winning move. The streak counts check-ins, tests, exercise and fluids, never health values. Logging a symptom completes the check-in, sick days pause the streak without resetting it, and no one is ranked against crewmates.

We built the Six Dots display: an ESP32-C6 screen with our own C++ firmware that shows the alert level as one to six dots. It gets the status over Wi-Fi from our backend, which runs the same rules, so it keeps working with the tablet off and flags a lost link.

Built with TypeScript, React and an offline PWA on the tablet, Kotlin and Spring Boot WebFlux for the ground station, C++ and PlatformIO on the ESP32, and whisper.cpp, llama.cpp and Piper for voice. Everything the crew uses runs on board, with no internet.

A local Qwen3.5-4B model lets the astronaut use the app by voice, with no internet. Tap the microphone and the app reads out a briefing built from its rules: each alert in its sourced words, then any missing readings and what is still due today. Ask “How is my breathing?” and it opens the matching screen.

In the morning check-in it asks each question, takes “yes” to confirm a value prefilled from a device, and saves only when the astronaut says “save”. Every answer stays visible on screen, and a tap always overrides voice. whisper.cpp turns speech into text in about a second, the model picks one command or value, and Piper reads the reply aloud.
